To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) when the discount rate is hyperbolic, the optimal policy under commitment may be very different from the set of Markover Perfect Equilibria; (2) when the discounting is hyperbolic and the probability of a catastrophic outcome is small, there may be multiple MPE and some may involve excessive stabilization effort; (3) the optimal policy under hyperbolaic discounting is more likely to involve a high level of stabilization effort than the set of Markow Perfect Equ

(a) under hyperbolic time preferences, a policy that stabilizes the climate at a low level of risk may be optimal even if the probability of a catastrophe is low, and (b) the set of MPE can include excessive and insufficient stabilization.

the optimal policy under hyperbopic discounting involves both a higher level of stabilization effort and a higher level of risk tolerance (i.e., willingness to accept a greater probability of catastrophe) than the optimal policy under constant discounting.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: How should society respond to climate change when it may be catastrophic?
the implications of hyperbolic discounters for the choice between stabilization policy and adaptation.
the question of whether climate change can be treated as a problem of intergenerational equity, as opposed to a problem of intertemporal efficiency.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
climate change is not a problem, but that it might become a problem, if we do not do something about it.
the optimal level of stabilization effort is not necessarily the same as the level implied by the MPE.
hyperbolic discounters should be more worried about climate change than time consistent agents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the distant future is more important than is commonly believed.
hyperbolic discounters should be concerned about climate change, but they should also be concerned that they may fail to act.
climate policy is much more complicated than it first appears.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the distant future matters in a way that it did not in the standard literature on time-consistent commitment to climate policy, even if we ignore the free-rider problems amongst contemporaneous decision makers.
the future is not a discounting parameter but a policy instrument.

when future generations are heavily discounted, the optimal policy may involve a much more rapid response to the threat of catastrophic climate change than would be the case if future generations were discounted at a lower rate.
